overview: The Shang is the first Chinese dynasty confirmed by contemporary written records, surviving on oracle bones and bronze inscriptions. Centered in the Anyang region, it controlled a network of towns and dependent settlements through ritual authority and bronze technology.

items.text: Oracle bone script, the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, carved on turtle shells and cattle scapulae for divination.
Horse-drawn war chariots appear in Shang burials at Anyang, adopted from steppe cultures.
Piece-mold bronze casting reaches its peak, producing ritual vessels weighing hundreds of kilograms.
The decimal system and a duodecimal cycle of days organized the Shang calendar.
Taotie masks and dragon motifs on bronze vessels show sophisticated design principles.
Jade carvings, marble sculptures and pottery figurines from royal tombs.
Musical instruments including bronze bells and stone chimes found in Anyang excavations.
The supreme deity Di ruled over lesser spirits and royal ancestors who mediated between heaven and earth.
Royal divination addressed questions of war, harvest, weather, illness and the king's activities.
Human sacrifice accompanied royal burials, with dozens or hundreds of victims in major tombs.
Millet and rice agriculture supported urban populations at Anyang and other centers.
Silk production evident from textile fragments found in bronze vessels.
The king hunted from chariots with bows and bronze-tipped arrows.
Cowrie shells from the Indian Ocean used as currency and prestige goods.
Tin and copper for bronze imported from distant sources.
Chinese writing system preserved in continuous use to the present day.
Bronze ritual vessel forms influenced Chinese metalwork for two thousand years.
The concept of a central royal authority over subordinate territories took root.

fall.text: King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king Zhou Xin at the Battle of Muye, ending the dynasty.
